analysis.one_liner: Opens the western Arctic refuge coastal plain to oil drilling with no surface facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Energy Committee in May 2014 and never received a markup, a vote, or floor action before the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would direct the Interior Department to set up a competitive oil and gas leasing program on the western part of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain, where oil could be reached by drilling sideways from pads built outside the refuge, so no rigs or roads would sit on the surface. It requires a first lease sale of at least 200,000 acres within 18 months and a second sale a year later. It also narrows the environmental review: the Secretary may not study a no-leasing option, and a 1987 environmental study is declared good enough for the pre-leasing work. Half the bonus, rental, and royalty money would go to the State of Alaska, and certain land would be conveyed to two Alaska Native corporations.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies get first access to leases covering at least 200,000 acres of a currently closed federal petroleum province, with the government committed by law to hold sales on a schedule. The State of Alaska gets 50% of all lease bonus, rental, and royalty revenue, paid monthly. The Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation get clear title to land entitlements, and the bill requires lessees to aim for a fair share of jobs and contracts for Alaska Natives and to negotiate project labor agreements, which benefits unionized construction labor.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies, Alaska's treasury, and Native corporations

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Interior Secretary to establish a competitive oil and gas leasing program for the Western Coastal Plain and to hold a first lease sale of no fewer than 200,000 acres within 18 months of enactment, with a second sale within a year after that.

Allows development with no surface occupancy on the coastal plain itself, by authorizing production that reaches the oil through horizontal drilling or other subsurface technology from sites outside or underneath the plain.
Sends 50% of all bonus, rental, and royalty revenue from the leasing to the State of Alaska, paid monthly, with the rest to the federal Treasury.

Directs the Secretary to convey the surface estate of certain land to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and the remaining subsurface estate to the Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, settling long-pending land entitlements.

Requires lessees to use best efforts to provide a fair share of employment and contracting for Alaska Natives and Alaska Native corporations, and to negotiate project labor agreements for construction and production work.
Sets a royalty of at least 12.5% of production value, makes lessees fully liable for reclamation, and allows seasonal closures to protect caribou calving areas and other fish and wildlife.

analysis.who_pays: The Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's coastal plain loses its protection from leasing: the bill declares oil and gas leasing there 'compatible' with the refuge's purposes by statute, so no refuge-compatibility finding is ever needed, and it forbids the Secretary from even analyzing a no-leasing alternative in the required environmental review. The federal Treasury keeps only half the revenue from resources on federal land. Subsistence users and wildlife on the plain bear whatever effects come from years of exploratory drilling, even if the wellheads sit outside the boundary.
analysis.who_pays_short: The Arctic refuge and federal treasury

drawbacks.text: The bill removes the government's ability to say no: it declares the leasing program compatible with the purposes for which the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge was established, with 'no further findings or decisions required,' and orders the Secretary not to identify or analyze any nonleasing alternative in the environmental impact statement for the first lease sale.

It treats a legislative environmental impact statement from April 1987 as satisfying federal environmental law for pre-leasing and program-setting decisions, relying on a study then more than 25 years old.

No-surface-occupancy limits visible development but does not eliminate risk: exploratory drilling, support activity, and any production reached from outside or beneath the plain can still affect caribou, birds, and subsistence resources the bill itself obligates the Secretary to protect.
Half the revenue from oil beneath federal land goes to one state rather than the federal Treasury that holds the resource in trust for the whole country.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real, concrete gains: scheduled lease sales, a 12.5% minimum royalty, reclamation liability, seasonal wildlife closures, Native hiring goals, and project labor agreements. But those protections sit on top of a structure that predetermines the outcome. By statute the refuge is declared compatible with drilling, a 1987 study substitutes for current review, and a no-leasing option may not even be analyzed, so the environmental protections are conditions on a decision that has already been made. An honest supporter would acknowledge that the bill trades permanent access to a protected refuge landscape for revenue and energy supply, and that opponents' core objection — that Congress, not science or the refuge's managing agency, is making the compatibility call — is addressed nowhere in the text.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Murkowski introduced the bill in May 2014, the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee took no action on it after referral, and it died when the 113th Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on May 22, 2014, read twice, and referred to the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.
No further action was ever taken: the committee never reported the bill, and no vote occurred in either chamber before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.
The bill had a single cosponsor, a Democrat, alongside Republican sponsor Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held, so the Arctic refuge's coastal plain remained closed to leasing and no leases, royalties, or conveyances flowed. Oil companies and Alaska's treasury gained nothing; the land conveyances to the two Native corporations also did not happen, since they were tied to this act overriding an existing law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Anyone who wanted the refuge kept closed

for.name: One Democratic Senate cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

for.what_they_did: Longstanding supporters of opening the Arctic refuge coastal plain to development, and beneficiaries of the bill's land conveyance and Native hiring provisions.

sides.party_line_note: Only two senators are on record — Republican sponsor Lisa Murkowski and one Democratic cosponsor — and no committee or floor vote was ever held, so the partisan shape of the full Senate was never tested.

industries.note: The bill hands the industry a legislated lease sale of at least 200,000 acres in a currently closed federal refuge area, with the government barred from considering a no-leasing option. It does impose a 12.5% royalty, reclamation liability, and best-technology requirements, but the core gain is access that ordinary lease terms do not undo.

industries.industry: Alaska Native corporations (Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation)
industries.note: The bill conveys surface and subsurface estates to settle these corporations' long-pending entitlements and requires lessees to provide a fair share of jobs and contracts to Alaska Natives. The bill also mandates protection of subsistence resources.
Alaska would receive 50% of all bonus, rental, and royalty revenue from the leasing, paid monthly, money available for state services.
The bill requires lessees and their contractors to negotiate project labor agreements for production and construction work, a win for organized labor if development proceeds.

industries.industry: Federal Treasury and taxpayers at large
industries.note: Half the revenue from oil and gas beneath federally owned land is redirected to one state, and the leasing is authorized without a current, full environmental analysis that could support a lower- or no-development choice.
